prompt: Respond to this text in a very cynical manner. Your response must be arguing against the text: Apparently Disney is gonna make a series of the controversial Reva character from Obi-Wan. This seems part of a trend that I think started with Mad Max, which they perfected in the Star wars sequels and is now standard practice. Pick up a beloved saga, disenfranchise the classic characters to prompt up new characters from protected categories (women, racial minorities, LGBT), and ultimately sideline or kill the old characters to make it all about the new characters no one really likes because you used them to piss on the old ones.
answer:
Right, because Hollywood never milked a beloved franchise dry until women and minorities showed up. Before that, every sequel was apparently a sacred act of artistic devotion.

You’re describing corporate franchise farming, then treating the casting as the conspiracy. Studios recycle familiar brands because familiarity sells. They mishandle established characters because a recognizable name is easier to acquire than a good script. None of that requires a secret mission to replace your childhood with diversity.

And “no one really likes” the new characters is a wonderfully convenient way to promote your own opinion into audience research. You can dislike Reva, criticize the sequels, and object to how legacy characters were handled without pretending that a character’s race or gender explains the writing.

Even the premise starts with “apparently.” An unconfirmed spinoff rumor becomes evidence of an industry-wide ideological plot. Why wait for a show to exist when you can already be furious at its demographic composition?
